title: Mental Control in Musical Imagery: A Dual Component Model
central_proposition: Mental control in musical imagery is a complex, multi-faceted process that can be broken down into two overarching components: initiation (how the experience begins) and management (control after it has begun).

concept_definitions.name: Mental control
concept_definitions.definition: an intriguing process involved in starting, stopping, shaping, and maintaining musical imagery

concept_definitions.name: Initiation
concept_definitions.definition: refers to whether the musical imagery experience began voluntarily or involuntarily

concept_definitions.name: Management
concept_definitions.definition: refers to attempts to control the musical imagery episode after it has begun (e.g., changing the song, stopping the experience)

argument_structure: The argument is built by first introducing musical imagery and the general concept of mental control. It then reviews four distinct literatures—lab-based auditory imagery, involuntary musical imagery, mental rehearsal and composition in musicians, and ecological musical imagery—analyzing how each implicitly or explicitly addresses aspects of mental control. This analysis reveals that mental control is not a unitary construct. The paper then synthesizes these findings into the proposed dual-component model, discusses its utility for re-interpreting past research, and outlines new directions for future research.
mechanism_or_causal_logic: The core mechanism is the decomposition of 'mental control' into two distinct, sequential, and potentially independent processes: `initiation` (the decision or spontaneity of starting an imagery episode) and `management` (the subsequent cognitive effort to sustain, alter, or stop the imagery). This distinction allows for a more nuanced understanding of how people interact with their internal musical experiences, recognizing that an experience can be involuntary in its start but still subject to conscious management, or vice versa. This framework provides a common language to integrate diverse findings and generate new research questions.

findings.consequent: Two distinct components: initiation and management
findings.mechanism: This decomposition allows for a more nuanced understanding of how musical imagery experiences unfold, change, or stop, recognizing that an episode can be involuntary in its start but still subject to conscious management.
findings.quote: Mental control can be further broken down into two primary components-initiation and management
findings.empirical_support_cited: Supported by analysis of four diverse literatures (lab-based auditory imagery, involuntary musical imagery, mental rehearsal/composition, ecological musical imagery).

findings.mechanism: Lab-based tasks demonstrate that people can form images of single tones, chords, or short passages of music at will when asked, suggesting a volitional initiation capacity.
findings.quote: Overall, this suggests people can initiate musical images when asked.
findings.empirical_support_cited: Farah and Smith (1983), Janata and Paroo (2006), Herholz et al. (2008) found people could form images with reasonable accuracy.

findings.mechanism: Tasks requiring participants to imagine the continuation of a musical passage and assess pitch/timing accuracy demonstrate the ability to maintain an image over time, though structural shifts in music can make it difficult.
findings.quote: Several studies also assess people's ability to manage their established images, such as deliberately sustaining the image
findings.empirical_support_cited: Hubbard (2018) review, Bailes and Bigand (2004), Janata and Paroo (2006), Herholz et al. (2008), Weir et al. (2015) show people can sustain images.

findings.consequent: Ability to manipulate and alter aspects of a musical image
findings.mechanism: Tasks involving changing pitch, transforming melodies (e.g., key, reversal), or adjusting tempo demonstrate that people can actively modify their musical imagery, with complexity affecting difficulty.
findings.quote: the more intuitive sense of management is the ability to manipulate and alter aspects of an image.
findings.empirical_support_cited: Hubbard and Stoeckig (1988), Gelding et al. (2015), Foster and Zatorre (2010), Foster et al. (2013) show manipulation abilities.

findings.antecedent: Higher self-reported imagery control (BAIS-Control subscale scores)
findings.consequent: Better accuracy on auditory imagery tasks (pitch judgments, sensorimotor synchronization)
findings.mechanism: Self-perception of control aligns with actual performance in some tasks, suggesting individual variations in the capacity to manage musical imagery.
findings.quote: higher self-reported imagery control predicted better accuracy... on auditory imagery tasks
findings.empirical_support_cited: Gelding et al. (2015), Greenspon et al. (2017), Colley et al. (2018) found correlations between BAIS-Control and performance.

findings.consequent: Ability to manage the experience (change content, end episode)
findings.mechanism: Even when musical imagery begins spontaneously, people often attempt to control it, suggesting that involuntary initiation does not preclude subsequent management.
findings.quote: involuntary musical imagery is a superordinate category that contains experiences such as earworms... key feature is that these experiences must be involuntarily initiated.
findings.empirical_support_cited: Beaman and Williams (2010, 2013), Williamson et al. (2014) show people engage in activities to get rid of earworms.

findings.consequent: Intentional initiation and management of musical imagery
findings.mechanism: Musicians purposefully initiate imagery (e.g., at specific times before performance) and manage it (e.g., running through pieces, constructing sound images, altering technical elements) to achieve performance and compositional goals.
findings.quote: Research examining musical imagery as part of the musical process... implies that control is a key component
findings.empirical_support_cited: Qualitative studies (Bowes, 2009; Holmes, 2005; Fine et al., 2015) and quantitative studies (Bernardi et al., 2013) on mental practice.

findings.consequent: Varying degrees of initiation and management
findings.mechanism: In daily life, musical imagery is often involuntary in initiation (~75% of the time), but people generally report moderate levels of perceived control over its management, indicating a dynamic interplay between the two components.
findings.quote: people do not frequently initiate musical imagery... but people report moderate levels of perceived control
findings.empirical_support_cited: Cotter et al. (2018) found ~25% voluntary initiation and moderate perceived control; Figure 1 shows management abilities.

testable_hypotheses_or_predictions: How do management behaviors differ between voluntarily and involuntarily initiated imagery?
Are purposefully initiated episodes easier to manage than involuntary initiated ones?
Which personal or environmental factors (e.g., mood, mental fatigue) most closely relate to attempts to control musical imagery?
Do these factors differ for initiation and management?
Future auditory imagery work could use more complex stimuli, such as music similar to what is heard in everyday life (e.g., pop songs), to evaluate people's control abilities.
Additional work should examine how realism of stimuli and related factors (e.g., stimulus complexity, familiarity, instrumental vs. vocal) relate to mental control.
Examination of how musicological factors (e.g., presence of lyrics, complexity of composition, musical genre) influence mental control abilities is a top candidate for future research.
Future ecological studies should work to adapt the behavioral approaches used in lab-based research to increase the validity of reports.
Empirically evaluate candidate sub-components of management (e.g., sustention, manipulation, termination).
Further develop theory regarding cognitive mechanisms involved in initiation and management.
bridge_warrants: The initiation and management distinction has antecedents in memory literature, distinguishing between direct (automated activation) and generative (actively accessing) memory retrieval as initiation-related distinctions.
Rehearsal of memory can be viewed as a management-related process, similar to musical imagery management.
In physical movement literature, research distinguishes between voluntary and involuntary actions, showing that involuntary actions can be brought under control, paralleling musical imagery.

Visual imagery and mind-wandering fields also have similar distinctions, with separate self-report measures for generating and manipulating visual images, and models differentiating how mind-wandering begins and unfolds.
The proposed dual-component model of mental control of musical imagery is grounded in these prior conceptualizations of control across memory, movement, visual imagery, and mind-wandering.
methodological_critiques: Lab-based auditory imagery work often lacks the complexity of musical imagery in everyday life and has limited ecological validity.
The ecological musical imagery approach, while assessing daily life experiences, often relies on descriptive and self-report nature, lacking the clarity and validity of lab-based studies.

The involuntary musical imagery literature lacks consistency in defining 'involuntary' and often obscures potential differences between involuntarily initiated imagery that remains involuntary and episodes that are deliberately managed.
The mental rehearsal and composition approach, rooted in music education, is almost completely isolated from the other musical imagery research approaches.

Past research has not explicitly developed the concept of mental control, often treating it as a unitary construct, and assessments of initiation or management tend to be a few items given only a passing mention.
model_structure: The proposed model is a dual-component framework for mental control in musical imagery, comprising two distinct, overarching components: `Initiation` and `Management`. Initiation refers to whether the musical imagery experience began voluntarily or involuntarily. Management refers to instances of control that occur after the experience has begun, encompassing sub-components such as sustaining the experience, altering its features (e.g., pitch, tempo, vocalist, instrument), or stopping the experience. The model suggests these components can operate independently, meaning an involuntarily initiated experience can still be subject to conscious management.
limitations: The model currently considers sustaining, altering, and stopping musical imagery as examples of management processes, but future research should investigate if these are sub-components or entirely separate components of management.

To date, no research has examined sustention, manipulation, and termination of musical imagery episodes individually, and further work is needed to understand how these dimensions of management relate to one another.

Research has yet to examine initiation and management within the same study, leaving the association between these two components and their differential relations with related concepts (e.g., affective valence) as an open issue.
